description: Buscamos integrantes interesados en programación, análisis y visualización de datos, sistemas de información geográfica (GIS), percepción remota, tecnología SAR y desarrollo web. También estamos abiertos a personas con conocimientos en ciencias de la Tierra, geografía, medio ambiente o comunicación científica.
summary:
Our project consists of an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), for which we developed a web platform where users can analyze changes in both temperature and chlorophyll levels. Through interactive graphs, these variables can be compared against the dates of specific human-made or natural events, allowing users to contrast, analyze, and interpret the resulting data.
This challenge requires giving a practical application to Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) technology. To address this, we created this accessible web tool—which you can explore below—to translate complex radar and remote sensing data into clear visual insights.
Finally, we believe this project is vital because there is a lack of human awareness regarding the environmental impact we cause. By simplifying access to satellite data, our platform aims to empower both researchers and the general public to better understand and protect our environment.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?

It is an interactive web map of the Gulf of Mexico (2003–2024) built on real satellite data. Users click a 1° cell or draw an area and get a floating window with:

sea surface temperature and chlorophyll, their anomalies and long-term trends;

depth and marine life records (OBIS);

the natural and human events that affected that area.

A timeline lets users replay the changes month by month. Every feature opens up/down tables, time series and 3D charts, and everything can be exported to Excel.

The project also uses synthetic aperture radar (SAR):

Sentinel-1 maps: possible oil slicks (sea surfaces smoothed by viscous films), ships and platforms, and radar-measured wind.

Before/after radar comparison for each event, such as hurricanes.

NISAR L-band slick detector: it flags areas where an oily film damps the small surface waves, so the radar echo drops, and rates each area by confidence.

A Python server (FastAPI) processes the data, and the page (Leaflet and Plotly) displays it in English or Spanish. A built-in Jupyter notebook lets researchers repeat and extend any analysis.

What are its benefits?

It turns complex satellite and radar data into clear maps, tables and charts that anyone can use, with no installation or account needed.

For researchers it offers rigorous analysis: anomalies against a 2003–2024 baseline, statistical trends with p-values, before/after event comparisons, and Excel and Jupyter exports.

It brings together sources that are normally scattered: NASA, ESA, JAXA, ISRO, NOAA and OBIS.

Radar sees through clouds and at night, so it can monitor oil slicks and storms when optical satellites cannot.

What is the expected impact of the project?

Raise awareness of how human activities (oil spills, industrial accidents, river diversions) and natural disasters (hurricanes, marine heatwaves, red tides) affect the Gulf of Mexico.

Help environmental impact assessments and specialized researchers find and download relevant data quickly.

Offer an early-warning, exploratory tool for possible oil slicks with NISAR, the newest NASA-ISRO radar mission. In testing it already pointed to known natural oil seeps in the Campeche Knolls.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

Languages and frameworks: Python 3.12 (FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, xarray, h5py, SQLAlchemy, openpyxl, matplotlib) and JavaScript/HTML/CSS (Leaflet, Plotly.js), with Jupyter and JupyterLite/Pyodide for in-browser notebooks.

Data:

NASA: JPL MUR SST, MODIS-Aqua chlorophyll, GIBS, NISAR and UAVSAR via NASA ASF DAAC.

Partner agencies: ESA Sentinel-1 and JAXA ALOS PALSAR, also via ASF.

Others: NOAA ETOPO1 and ERDDAP, and OBIS.

Development: a Windows 11 PC, Git/GitHub, and generative AI (Claude Code) as a tool to generate code and link resources.

Hosting: Render, with code published under the MIT license.

How is your project creative?

It connects three viewpoints that are usually separate: ocean color and temperature, radar and a timeline of real events. This lets users explore relationships between environmental changes and disasters.

Instead of downloading entire 6 GB NISAR files, it reads only the needed parts over the internet (about 30 MB). That makes radar-based slick detection possible on a regular computer.

It is inspired by platforms such as Copernicus Marine and NASA Earthdata, but focused on one region and one question: how human and natural events change the Gulf.

It shows uncertainty openly: confidence levels, “calm sea / stormy weather” warnings and a reminder that coincidence does not imply causation. It also incorporates advice from an aquaculture bioengineer on how to present the data.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered several factors for the website, starting with key parameters such as temperature and chlorophyll, all the way to bright objects like ships and oil platforms, and even wind measured by radar. We also included the idea of a language translation feature for both Spanish and English speakers, alongside a section for natural or human-made events, and a chart that provides data we can compare and analyze.

When searching for information, we prioritized NASA data websites, always saving the links for future reference and ensuring they were open-source.
